question: Which of the following nail findings is characteristically associated with chronic arsenic poisoning?

answers.text: Mees' lines (transverse white bands across all nails)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mees' lines are transverse white bands in the nails corresponding to episodes of acute arsenic poisoning. Each band represents a discrete toxic insult; multiple parallel bands indicate repeated exposures. They are a key post-mortem and clinical forensic finding in arsenicosis.
Incorrect. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped, concave nails) indicates iron-deficiency anaemia or haemochromatosis. It is not associated with arsenic poisoning.
Incorrect. Leukonychia totalis (completely white nails) is associated with hypoalbuminaemia (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome) or Terry's nails in chronic illness. It is not specific to arsenic.
Incorrect. Yellow nail syndrome is associated with lymphoedema, chronic respiratory disease (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis), and rheumatoid arthritis — not with arsenic or metal poisoning.

overallFeedback.feedback: Mees' lines are the correct answer for arsenic. Heavy metal nail/skin markers: arsenic = Mees' lines + raindrop pigmentation; lead = Burton's blue gum line; mercury = acrodynia (pink disease in children); copper = green hair discolouration.

Correct. Mees' lines (arsenic), Burton's line (lead, blue gum line), Acrodynia pink rash (mercury in children) — each heavy metal has its signature clinical marker. Mees' lines are also seen in thallium poisoning.
